title: FADDIR Test | Femoroacetabular Impingement Assessment | Labral Tear
purpose: Screening test for femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) and labral tears of the hip.
structure: Hip joint: CAM morphology (bony prominence on the femoral neck), pincer morphology (acetabular retroversion or over-pronounced labrum), most often a combination; acetabular labrum.
procedure: Patient supine. The examiner flexes the hip to 90°, adducts it and adds internal rotation (Flexion-ADDuction-Internal Rotation).
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar hip/groin pain.

accuracy.source: Reiman et al. 2015 systematic review/meta-analysis (moderate-quality studies)

notes: Useful for exclusion screening only; a positive test cannot diagnose FAI. FAI morphology is often asymptomatic, even in athletes, but is linked to higher osteoarthritis risk. Related tests on the page: Thomas test, anterior/posterior labral tear tests, McCarthy test, foot progression angle walking test.

title: Patrick's Test / FABER Test / Figure Four Test for Hip OA & SIJ Pain
purpose: Assess limited hip range in horizontal adduction (commonly limited in hip osteoarthritis) and provoke pain from the hip or the sacroiliac joint.
structure: Hip joint (Flexion-ABduction-External Rotation position) and sacroiliac joint; pain usually felt in the Fortin area/posterior SIJ line for SIJ pain or in the groin for hip pain.
procedure: Patient supine, examiner on the affected side. The patient flexes the ipsilateral knee and places the medial heel against the other knee. The examiner fixates the contralateral ASIS while the patient lowers the ipsilateral knee toward the table as far as possible, foot staying on the other knee. Finally the examiner applies overpressure at the ipsilateral knee of 15 kg for 5 seconds.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar pain (Fortin area/posterior SIJ line for SIJ, groin for hip).

accuracy.source: Schneider et al. 2020 (SIJ); reliability: intra-rater ICC 0.93 Ross et al. 2003, inter-rater kappa 0.47 Sutlive et al. 2008

notes: Page rates it weak clinical value both as a hip provocation test (low inter-rater reliability) and as an SIJ test. Also part of the Cluster of Sutlive for hip OA; listed as an adductor longus length test on the Ely's page.

title: External Rotation Stinchfield Test | Core Muscle Injury Assessment
purpose: Assess core muscle injury (CMI, athletic pubalgia, 'sports hernia'), which falls under pubic-related groin pain in the Doha classification.
structure: Abdominal wall weakening/tearing without a true hernia plus injury at the insertion of adductor longus and rectus abdominis on the pubis.
procedure: Patient supine, affected leg fully extended and placed in external rotation. The patient lifts the leg off the table against the examiner's resistance.

accuracy.source: Kurowicki et al. 2020 diagnostic cohort (one of 3 proposed tests)

notes: Weak clinical value as a stand-alone test; use within a cluster (page lists straight leg sit-up and resisted cross-body sit-up tests) together with history and diagnostic ultrasound. Differentiate from FAI, lumbar referral and SIJ pain.

title: Anterior Labral Tear Test | Hip Labral Tear Assessment
purpose: Assess anterior-superior impingement, anterior labral tear and iliopsoas tendonitis of the hip.
procedure: Bring the hip into flexion, external rotation and abduction, then slowly move it into internal rotation, adduction and extension.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's symptoms, with or without a click, or pain.

accuracy.source: n/a: page states no diagnostic studies have evaluated reliability or validity

notes: Clinical value unknown. No references listed on the page.

title: Posterior Labral Tear Test of the Hip | Hip Labral Tear Assessment
purpose: Assess posteroinferior hip impingement, posterior labral tears and anterior hip instability.
procedure: Patient supine with a neutral spine. The examiner brings the hip into maximal flexion, adduction and internal rotation, then slowly moves it into abduction, external rotation and extension.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar groin pain, with or without a click.

accuracy.source: n/a: page states no diagnostic studies have evaluated reliability or validity

notes: Clinical value unknown. No references listed on the page.

title: Hip Prone Instability Test | Hip Microinstability Assessment
purpose: Assess hip microinstability, a relatively new clinical entity in young patients.
structure: Hip stabilizers: acetabulum, labrum, ligamentum teres, capsuloligamentous complex and surrounding muscles. Proposed mechanism: repetitive axial and/or rotational loading with anatomic abnormalities; traumatic and atraumatic onsets described.
procedure: Patient prone, examiner on the unaffected side. Flex the affected knee to 90° as a lever, place the other hand on the posterior aspect of the greater trochanter, then externally rotate the leg while applying a downward (anteriorly directed) force at the greater trochanter.

accuracy.source: Hoppe et al. 2017 (first validity study, with limitations; page rates moderate clinical value)

notes: Combine with history and Beighton score for hyperlaxity. Related tests: AB-HEER, HEER, foot progression walking angle.

title: Thomas Test for Iliopsoas Tightness
purpose: Muscle length test for iliopsoas shortening; also described in the literature as a test for FAI.
structure: Iliopsoas (hip flexor); iliotibial tract if the J-sign appears.
procedure: Patient supine. The patient pulls the non-tested leg toward the chest until the lumbar lordosis flattens, while the tested leg stays extended on the table.
positive: The extended leg lifts off the table and the patient feels a stretch in the groin. Adduction of the extended leg (J-sign) may indicate iliotibial tract shortening.

accuracy.lr_plus: 11.1 (for variable hip pathologies such as FAI)
accuracy.lr_minus: 0.12 (for variable hip pathologies such as FAI)
accuracy.source: McCarthy et al. 1995; reliability reference Peeler & Anderson 2007

notes: Only moderately useful because asymptomatic FAI findings are prevalent; iliopsoas shortening cannot be reliably detected visually or with a goniometer. Other length tests listed: Ober's, Ely's, Kendall, 90-90 SLR, backsaver sit and reach, tripod sign, Phelps.

title: Ober's Test for Iliotibial Band Tightness
purpose: Assess tightness of the tensor fasciae latae / iliotibial band.
structure: Tensor fasciae latae and iliotibial band; per Willett et al. 2016 the findings are actually influenced by gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and the hip joint capsule.
procedure: Patient side-lying, lower hip and knee flexed for stability. The examiner fixates the pelvis with one hand, passively abducts the upper leg and brings it into slight extension, then slowly lowers it toward the table. Originally described with 90° knee flexion; Physiotutors prefer the upper leg fully extended for more stretch.
positive: The upper leg stays in the air and does not drop down to the table.

accuracy.source: n/a (Willett et al. 2016 anatomic study questions validity)

notes: Willett et al. 2016 refute that the ITB limits hip adduction in either version of the test and question its validity for ITB tightness; interpret with caution.

title: Ely's Test | Rectus Femoris Contracture | Rectus Femoris Length
purpose: Muscle length test for rectus femoris flexibility/contracture.
structure: Rectus femoris (AIIS to tibial tuberosity, crossing hip and knee).
procedure: Patient prone. The examiner passively flexes the knee maximally.
positive: Spontaneous hip flexion (buttock rises) on maximal knee flexion, compensating for a short rectus femoris, or pain during the test.

accuracy.source: Reliability only: Peeler & Anderson 2008, positive/negative scoring intra-rater kappa 0.52, inter-rater kappa 0.46 (moderate); with goniometer intra-rater ICC 0.69, inter-rater ICC 0.66

notes: Page lists other length tests: Thomas (iliopsoas), Kendall (rectus femoris), 90-90 SLR (hamstrings), Phelps (gracilis), Ober's (TFL/ITB), piriformis test, Patrick's (adductor longus).

title: 90-90 Straight Leg Raise Test | Active Knee Extension Test | Hamstring Length
purpose: Assess hamstring length and possible hamstring contracture (also called Active Knee Extension Test, AKET).
procedure: Patient supine with hips and knees flexed to 90° and lumbar spine neutral; the patient holds the back of the thighs to stabilize. The patient then actively extends the knee on the tested side while keeping the lumbar spine neutral.
positive: The page gives no explicit positive criterion; the outcome is the knee extension deficit (degrees short of full extension) compared between sides.

accuracy.source: Reliability only: Neto et al. 2015, intra-rater ICC 0.91 (excellent), smallest detectable difference 7-8°

notes: Other hamstring length tests on the page: backsaver sit and reach, tripod sign.

title: Tripod Sign | Hamstring Length Assessment
structure: Hamstrings; must be differentiated from nerve root involvement.
procedure: Patient seated with knees flexed 90° over the edge of the bench. The examiner passively extends one knee, returns it, then repeats on the other side and compares.
positive: The patient leans the trunk backward to relieve hamstring tension when the knee is fully extended. Shooting pain down the whole leg instead of muscular tension suggests a nerve root problem, not a positive test.
notes: Other length tests listed: Ober's (TFL), Ely's (rectus femoris), Phelps (gracilis), 90-90 SLR, Kendall, backsaver sit and reach, Thomas.

title: Phelps Test | Gracilis Length Testing
purpose: Muscle length test for gracilis contracture/shortening.
structure: Gracilis, the only biarticular muscle of the adductor group (crosses hip and knee).
procedure: Patient prone with knees extended. The examiner passively abducts both hips as far as possible, then asks the patient to flex the knees to 90° and tries to abduct further passively.
positive: Abduction increases after 90° knee flexion (knee flexion slackens gracilis, so more abduction becomes available if gracilis was the limiting factor).
notes: Other length tests listed: Ober's, Ely's, Kendall, 90-90 SLR, backsaver sit and reach, tripod sign, Thomas.
